title: Executive & Board Leadership
subtitle: Communicate AI as strategy, risk, capital, and organizational change
summary: Learn to communicate with CEOs and boards using business language, decision memos, scenario planning, governance reporting, and concise executive narratives.

lessons.title: Board-level AI narrative
lessons.body: A board needs clarity on strategic stakes, investment, material risks, governance, capability maturity, competitors, and key decisions—not a model architecture tutorial.

lessons.title: Decision memos
lessons.body: Use a one- or two-page format: decision required, context, options, recommendation, economics, risk, assumptions, reversibility, and next checkpoint. Make uncertainty explicit.

lessons.title: AI maturity reporting
lessons.body: Create a balanced executive scorecard covering business value, adoption, delivery, platform health, governance, incidents, talent, and pipeline. Avoid vanity metrics such as raw prompt counts.

quiz.q: Management’s pilot budget has three months left. Quality is promising, but finance has not verified net value and no scale decision is due today. Which board request most clearly separates oversight from management’s next evidence task?
options: Authorize the full scale envelope now, while management returns with net-value evidence before committing vendor contracts
Approve one model and a common accuracy threshold now, leaving management to verify value within the remaining pilot budget
Confirm the strategic risk and spending boundaries, require a dated net-value gate, and retain management’s delegated pilot decisions
Approve each pilot’s revised release plan now, reserving capital discussion for the first quarter with realized benefits
quiz.explanation: The immediate oversight issue is whether management is operating within acceptable strategy, exposure, and capital limits while closing an evidence gap. A dated return gate avoids premature scale authorization; directors do not need to select models or perform delegated release management.

quiz.q: A pilot’s draft time falls from 24 to 17 minutes, corrections rise from 6% to 11%, and cost per correct case rises from CAD 4.20 to CAD 4.80. The comparison is representative but cause is unproven. Which board row most accurately turns these facts into an investment decision?
options: Show all three changes; service VP holds expansion while evaluation and finance examine rework and return in two weeks
Show all three changes; service VP expands to recover fixed cost while evaluation investigates corrections and returns in two weeks
Show all three changes; service VP attributes the higher cost to review, asks finance to exclude it, and returns in two weeks
Show all three changes; service VP reports seven minutes of realized cash savings while finance checks staffing and returns in two weeks
quiz.explanation: The representative comparison shows faster drafting alongside worse corrections and unit cost, so a temporary expansion hold and dated investigation fit the mixed evidence. The other rows infer an unproven cause, exclude a real cost, or treat time as cash before staffing effects are established.

quiz.q: An EU deployment row has counsel’s completed review for internal draft advice using existing employee permissions. The requested extension would display answers directly to customers, using the same model and sources. Which revised row accurately represents the current evidence?
options: EU customer advice: existing role and data review complete; product owner evaluates the translated interface before the release date
EU customer advice: internal review complete; service owner carries its classification and tests customer satisfaction before the release date
EU customer advice: source access review complete; risk owner accepts external-output risk within the existing internal release approval
EU customer advice: internal assessment remains scoped; local counsel and product owners reassess the changed use and quality before release
quiz.explanation: The completed internal assessment is useful evidence but has a documented scope that excludes direct customer answers. Reassessing the intended use and customer-quality boundary with the authorized owners preserves that distinction; unchanged technical components do not prove the legal or operational assessment transfers.

quiz.q: A buy option originally sent claim text to a vendor. Privacy now permits a redesigned route that sends de-identified extracts only, but local preprocessing and review add costs absent from the comparison. Buying was previously cheaper than API build. What should the memo recommend next?
options: Choose buying because permission has been resolved, and absorb the extra local work within the existing contingency
Re-cost and evaluate the permitted design against build and defer on the same outcome and horizon before selecting a route
Choose API build because buying’s original data design failed, using the original buy quote as its cost comparison
Rank buying with a lower privacy-risk score, leaving added review costs for the operating owner after the procurement decision
quiz.explanation: The permitted redesign removes one constraint but changes both workflow cost and potentially quality. Reconcile those inputs on a common basis before recommending buy, build, or defer; an earlier price advantage cannot establish the new route’s economics.

quiz.q: A memo forecasts 30,000 annual eligible cases, 60% adoption, five net minutes released per adopted case, and CAD 48 per usable hour. The permitted route also costs CAD 24,000 fixed annually and CAD 2 per adopted case. Exclude setup and other benefits. What annual result, before any cash-realization decision, should the option table show?
options: CAD 72,000 net capacity value, using all released time at the stated hourly value
CAD 48,000 net capacity value, deducting fixed cost because variable work is already staffed
CAD 12,000 net capacity value, deducting both fixed and adopted-case operating costs
CAD 36,000 net capacity value, deducting per-case costs because fixed cost is shared
quiz.explanation: 18,000 adopted cases release 1,500 hours worth CAD 72,000. Stated operating cost is CAD 24,000 + 18,000 × CAD 2 = CAD 60,000, leaving CAD 12,000 net capacity value before setup; a staffing or other operational decision is still needed for a cash claim.

quiz.q: A pilot passes its quality floor for routine cases but fails on complex cases. Its approved expansion gate required both, and the financial forecast assumes all case types. The team proposes a routine-only extension within the remaining cap. Which memo best supports that decision?
options: Approve routine expansion now and preserve the original benefit forecast while complex-case work continues
Continue the full pilot with extra complex-case review, treating the routine pass as enough evidence for the next tranche
Defer any further work until complex cases pass, retaining the original scope and spending the cap on interface improvements
Propose a revised routine-only gate and net-value forecast, retain complex-case fallback, and seek approval for the bounded extension
quiz.explanation: Routine evidence can support a narrower proposal, but that is a changed scope with changed volumes, costs, and benefits. The decision maker should approve its specific gate and cap; retaining the full-scope forecast or inferring an all-case pass from one segment would conflict with the original terms.

quiz.q: Twenty registered material uses include 16 with current evaluations. Audit finds five further material uses, two already evaluated under the same criterion. What coverage should be reported for all known material uses?
options: 72%, from 18 current evaluations among 25 known uses, with discovered gaps assigned for remediation
80%, from 16 current evaluations among 20 registered uses, with the five additions listed in the audit appendix
64%, from 16 current evaluations among 25 known uses, excluding evaluations outside the registered process
60%, from 18 current evaluations among 30 uses, adding the five discoveries to both the current and prior inventory
quiz.explanation: There are 25 known material uses and 18 current evaluations under the stated common criterion, giving 72%. A registered-only denominator hides known exposure, while excluding valid newly discovered evaluations understates coverage; the inventory expansion and outstanding owners should be explicit.

quiz.q: An executive dashboard reports zero AI incidents. Only 6 of 20 material uses have a tested reporting route, reviewer scenario checks show weak failure recognition, and another rollout asks for funding. Which recommendation best uses the dashboard’s evidence?
options: Expand rollout under the zero-incident result and fund awareness training, with reporting-route coverage checked after launch
Treat zero incidents as low-confidence evidence, fund detection and reviewer competence, and condition expansion on tested readiness
Commission an incident audit for the six tested uses, retaining expansion because those systems establish the central process works
Set a higher incident-count target to encourage reporting, fund the new rollout, and use later reports to prioritize control improvements
quiz.explanation: Zero reported incidents is weak assurance when detection, recognition, and reporting cover only part of the portfolio. Funding those capability gaps and establishing a readiness gate improves the evidence before exposure grows; a numerical reporting target or successful route in six uses does not establish coverage for the others.

quiz.q: A team changes adoption from monthly login to correct eligible-workflow completion. Last year’s logs lack workflow outcomes, so a reliable backcast is unavailable. Which reporting proposal best preserves useful history without fabricating comparability?
options: Backcast the new measure using current completion-to-login ratios, then connect the historical and new series
Connect the two observed series with a documented definition break and describe the old and new percentages as one trend
Replace historical percentages with estimated completions from manager recall, attaching a low-confidence label
Preserve the old series, start the new measure separately, and show both during overlap with the data gap explained
quiz.explanation: A disclosed break helps, but the two percentages still measure different behaviors and should not be treated as one comparable trend. Preserve actual history and collect an overlap period; applying current ratios or recalled outcomes to missing past data would add unsupported assumptions to the main metric.

homework: Prepare a 10-slide board update on enterprise AI: market context, strategy, portfolio, value realized, material risks, governance, platform, workforce, 12-month roadmap, and 3 decisions requested from the board.
